mcqs.question: You need to support "cancel this order" in a REST API where cancellation has side effects (refund, notification) beyond a simple field change. What's the most REST-consistent way to model it?
options: POST /orders/1024/cancellations — model the action itself as a sub-resource you create
DELETE /orders/1024 — deleting the order is close enough to cancelling it
GET /orders/1024/cancel — a GET is safe to call so it's fine for triggering the cancellation
PUT /orders/1024 with a raw verb string in the body, e.g. {"action": "cancel"}
mcqs.explanation: Modeling the action as a created sub-resource keeps the noun-first discipline and gives the action its own addressable record. DELETE would remove the order entirely, not cancel it; GET must never cause a side effect since it's assumed safe and cacheable; a raw action string in a PUT body reintroduces RPC-style verbs through the back door.

mcqs.question: A client sends a malformed request body to an endpoint. The server returns 200 OK with {"error": "invalid field 'email'"} in the JSON body. What's wrong with this?
options: It should be a 500 Internal Server Error since something went wrong
It defeats tooling and clients that branch on the HTTP status line rather than parsing every body for an error field
Nothing — as long as the client parses the body correctly, the status code doesn't matter
JSON error bodies are never allowed in REST APIs
mcqs.explanation: A 200 status tells every generic client, cache, and monitor 'this succeeded' — so anything relying on the status line (not custom body parsing) will treat a client error as a success. The right code here is a 4xx (400 for malformed input), not 5xx, since the fault is the client's request, not the server. JSON error bodies are fine; the status code just also has to be honest.

mcqs.question: A service exposes a single operation, runNightlyReconciliation, with no natural "resource" behind it — it just triggers a batch job. What does the compare slide suggest?
options: Force it into a REST resource shape anyway, since consistency always beats fit
REST is strictly required for any production API regardless of the operation's shape
An RPC-style or hybrid endpoint is often the more honest choice when the operation isn't resource-shaped
Use a GET request since it's the simplest HTTP verb available
mcqs.explanation: The slide's decision rule is to match the style to the domain: genuinely resource-shaped operations benefit from REST's conventions, but a one-off command with no natural noun is often better served by an RPC-style or hybrid endpoint rather than a forced, awkward resource model. Neither REST nor GET is mandatory here.

mcqs.question: Two endpoints in the same API, /deleteUser and /deleteUserOrder, return different status codes on success (one 200 with a body, one 204 with none). What underlying problem does this reveal?
options: Nothing — each endpoint is free to choose whatever status code fits its own logic
204 is invalid for any DELETE request and must be fixed first
The problem is only cosmetic and has no effect on client code
The verb-in-URL pattern has let each endpoint invent its own inconsistent convention instead of sharing one
mcqs.explanation: Baking verbs into URLs tends to produce a pile of one-off endpoints, each with its own status-code habits, forcing clients to write bespoke handling per endpoint instead of one shared '2xx succeeded' path. 204 is a perfectly valid DELETE response; the real issue is the lack of a shared convention, which very much does affect client code, not just cosmetics.
